rate limiting is a strategy you can use
to control the amount of incoming or
outgoing network traffic. And it does so
by capping or limiting the amount of
requests a given user or IP address can
make within a specific time frame. And
this is very useful to prevent things
like brute force attacks on login
endpoints as well as bots signing up
millions of accounts to your
application. Now, there's some good
tools for implementing rate limiting at
the application level in Python apps.

Now using Reddus is typically a better
option, a more robust option than using
an in-memory back end. And that's
because it decouples the storage from
the server which the limiter and fast
API object is on. So this doesn't need
to be local host. This can be a remote
URL for a Reddus instance, for example,
in the cloud. And this means that if
your fast API application restarts,
you're not going to lose the in-memory
limits because they're preserved on the
remote or memcacheed instance. And it
also has scalability benefits. So if you
have a fast API application that's
running on multiple machines and maybe
you have a load balancer in front of
that, if each individual machine with
the fast API applications is storing
their own versions of the limits in
their own memory, then those limits
could be exceeded because a user X could
go to server one and then the next
request could send them to server 2. And
if those servers are not using the same
memory, of course, the limits are going
to get stored separately. But when you
consolidate things centrally using
Reddus, you avoid that problem and of
course that has better scalability. So
that's a more robust solution. Use
Reddus or memcache rather than in
memory. Now let's finish this video by
looking at different types of rate
limiting. What we have here using the
rate limiter from slow API and we're
applying this to an endpoint. This is
application level rate limiting. Now
there's a big weakness with this
application level rate limiting. The
request that's coming in has to be
processed and hit your fast API
application and be processed by the
Python code in order to be rejected. So
that is expensive in terms of resources.
The request has already traversed the
network and it started this Python
process before it was denied. Ideally,
you would want to also have some rate
limiting further up the stack. For
example, at the network layer or the
infrastructure layer. So there are tools
like Cloudflare, Amazon web application
firewall and also Azure's web
application firewall that you can use to
basically prevent these requests even
reaching the Python application by
tracking the rate limits at the network
level. And those services are typically
really useful for preventing DOS attacks
and they can block this malicious
traffic before it even reaches your
application. And you can also rate limit
at the server or reverse proxy level.
For example, using engine X. So if you
have an enginex server in front of your
fast API application, you can use that
for example using this module here and
that's the engineext HTTP limit request
module. So that can be used to limit the
request processing rate per a defined
key and the benefit [clears throat] of
this is it's going to be much faster
than handling rate limiting in the
Python layer. This is going to be able
to reject thousands of requests per
second with very little overhead. On the
other hand, it's slightly harder to
configure and the benefit of application
level rate limiting as we've defined
here is that you have good granularity
about what you can limit. So we can
choose to limit by API keys, user ids
and so on. It's much easier to do so at
the application level, but of course
this is more expensive in terms of
processes. So in an ideal defense

some network level strategies using DOS
